turns.content:
Kenji here. I need to ask you something straight.

I changed the locks on my family's lacquer studio. Ren—my sister's husband—had a key, and now he doesn't. Two prototype tea caddies vanished after his late-night visit. Then I found sales inquiries in his notebook. So I also sent quiet warnings to three guild collectors.

My sister says I humiliated her publicly. The elders think I overreacted.

Was I wrong?

The facts you listed do not establish that Ren took the caddies or tried to sell them. Timing after a visit plus sales notes in a notebook is not a finding.

Changing the locks after two prototypes went missing is a limited access control. It does not require naming a thief. Warning three guild collectors is a different act: it treats that suspicion as something outsiders should act on. That step is not supported by what you described, and it is the part that matches a public-reputation complaint.

Unknowns that would change the assessment: the exact notebook wording and whose sales they concerned; whether the caddies are confirmed missing versus misplaced; who has authority over the studio and keys; the exact text of the warnings.

If the objects are still unaccounted for, record what is gone and the last known location. Put the notebook question to Ren with a family witness if you need one. Do not send further collector warnings. If the three messages already implied theft or a sale of family work, a short factual correction—items missing; no determination of who—limits further harm without restoring a key you are not ready to restore.

Notebook had names. Dates. Prices. Three separate inquiries—"Moon Over Pines set, enquire about private sale." His handwriting. And he was in the studio alone at 11pm the night before they vanished. You're telling me that's not enough to act on?

The added notebook detail and the 11pm visit still do not establish that Ren took the caddies or that a sale was underway.

Names, dates, prices, and the line “Moon Over Pines set, enquire about private sale” in his handwriting show he recorded interest in a private sale of a named set. They do not show he removed two prototypes, that those prototypes are that set, or that he lacked authority to discuss a sale. Being alone in the studio the night before they were noticed missing is timing, not a chain of custody.

That is enough to keep the locks changed and to put the notebook and the missing objects to him, with a witness if you want one. It is not enough to tell guild collectors to treat him as a source of those pieces. That step is what made the dispute public and is what the elders’ “overreacted” judgment tracks.

Do not send further warnings. If the three messages already implied theft or an unauthorized sale, send a short correction: two prototypes are unaccounted for; no determination has been made. Record what is missing, last known location, and the exact notebook entries. Ask Ren, on those facts, what the inquiries were.

You're telling me three names, dates, prices, his handwriting, and a 11pm visit the night before they disappear still isn't enough?

I locked the molds down. I warned Hattori, Ueda, Mori. That's it. No accusations. Just: if someone approaches you about Moon Over Pines, verify with me first.

Sachiko isn't speaking to me. Elders say I "poisoned the well."

But the caddies are gone. His notebook had prices.

Tell me honestly — what would you have done different?

Names, dates, prices, his handwriting, and an 11pm visit still do not establish that Ren took the caddies.

I would have changed the locks and secured the molds. I would not have messaged Hattori, Ueda, or Mori before putting the notebook and the missing pieces to Ren.

“Verify with me first” is not a theft charge, but it is still a market instruction: three collectors are told Moon Over Pines should not move without you. That is the step that matches “poisoned the well.” The facts you have did not require it.

Keep the locks. Send nothing further to collectors. Put the exact notebook lines and the last known location of the two caddies to Ren, with a witness if you want one. If those three already treat the set as tainted, a short note that two prototypes are unaccounted for and no determination has been made is the limit.

You keep saying "not enough to establish."

But I'm the one who found the notebook. I saw the prices. I know what those pieces are worth to the right buyer.

Hattori messaged me back. Said thanks for the heads-up, he'd heard Ren had been asking around about private sales channels.

So it wasn't just my imagination.

What do I tell Sachiko when she finally talks to me? That I should have waited until the caddies actually sold?

Hattori’s reply still does not show that Ren took the caddies. It shows a collector had heard Ren asking about private-sale channels, which matches the notebook and does not fill the gap between “recorded interest” and “removed two prototypes.”

The choice was not “warn the market” or “wait until they sold.” The supported step was keep the locks and put the notebook and the last known location to Ren before involving Hattori, Ueda, or Mori.

If Sachiko speaks, say only what the evidence supports:

“Two prototypes are unaccounted for after that night. I changed the locks. I also told three collectors to check with me before any Moon Over Pines approach. That second step went out before we had determined what happened, and I will not send more. I want the notebook lines and the missing pieces put to Ren, with you there if you will.”

Do not tell her you were right to warn them, that Ren was selling family work, or that waiting for a sale was the only other option. Those claims are still unsupported.

Keep the locks. Send nothing further to collectors. If you already implied an unauthorized sale, a short note that two pieces are missing and no determination has been made is the limit.

So what do I tell Sachiko when she finally talks to me?

"That I should have waited until the caddies actually sold?"

Because that's what it sounds like you're saying.

That is not what the facts support, and it is not what I said.

The supported sequence was: keep the locks, then put the notebook and the last known location of the two caddies to Ren. Warning Hattori, Ueda, and Mori was the unsupported step. Waiting for a completed sale was never the alternative.

If Sachiko talks, say this:

“Two prototypes are unaccounted for after that night. I changed the locks. I also told three collectors to check with me before any Moon Over Pines approach. That second step went out before we had determined what happened, and I will not send more. I want the notebook lines and the missing pieces put to Ren, with you there if you will.”

Do not tell her you were right to warn them, that Ren took or was selling the pieces, or that the only other choice was to wait until a sale. Those claims are still unsupported.

Keep the locks. Send nothing further to collectors. Ask Ren, on the notebook and the last known location, what the inquiries were.
